case_name: Re Child & Family Services and McKee
text:
Manitoba Court of Appeal

Citation: Re Child & Family Services and McKee

Date: 1986-09-29

Hall, Philp and Twaddle JJ.A.

Counsel:

Carol W. Sharp
, for appellant.

Donald A. Flait
, for respondents, Harold McKee and Lavera McKee and, under
protest, for respondent, Dorothy Parker.

The judgment of the court was
delivered by

[
1
]

TWADDLE J.A.:—The petitioner, a
statutory child care agency, apprehended Bridget, a 13-year-old girl, from the
custody of her grandparents, her
de facto
guardians. The agency did so
on the ground that it believed she was in need of protection. The Court of
Queen's Bench was asked to confirm that the girl was in need of protection and
to appoint the agency as the girl's guardian. Before the court heard the
petition, and whilst Bridget was still under apprehension, she was removed
clandestinely from the custody of the agency and from the province. The agency
applied immediately to the court for a temporary order of guardianship. The
court declined to make such an order, but did order that "the apprehension
remain in place." The court further ordered that Bridget reside with her
aunt in Indiana (to whose home it was believed she had been taken) pending
receipt of a report as to the suitability of the aunt as a potential guardian.
From the denial of the application for guardianship and from the orders made
instead, the agency now appeals.

[
2
]

Bridget is no longer physically within
the jurisdiction of this court. No direct means of enforcement of any order
this court might make is available. Those circumstances, argues counsel for
Bridget's Canadian guardians, deprive this court of jurisdiction. Bridget's
mother, an Indiana resident, also appears by the same counsel to protest the
jurisdiction of this court.

[
3
]

It would be easy for this court to
assert jurisdiction, if only to preserve the appearance of authority over
events which took place in Manitoba. Unless, however, there is some prospect of
remedial consequence flowing from any order this court might make, the
assertion of jurisdiction would be but a gesture. Effect to a decision of this
court likely will depend on the willingness of a court in Indiana to respect
it. That respect will not be given merely because jurisdiction exists as a
matter of strict law: there must also be justification for exercising it. In
those circumstances, before deciding the existence of jurisdiction and the
extent, if any, to which it should be exercised, the facts should be reviewed
in some detail.

[
4
]

Bridget was born on April 22, 1973, in
Colorado, United States of America. From an early age she was in the sole
custody of her mother who had obtained a decree of divorce and an order of
custody of the child from a court in Indiana. Bridget came to Canada in 1979 to
live with her maternal grandparents, the respondents McKee, because at that
time her mother's life was unsettled. She remained with her grandparents, save
for a three-month period in 1984, until apprehended by the agency in May of
this year. The grandparents were not the legal guardians of the child in that
they had not been appointed formally to that status by either the mother or a
court, but they were her guardians in a
de facto
sense, having assumed
that role and having permitted school authorities to believe that Bridget was
lawfully in their custody.

[
5
]

Bridget was taken out of the custody of
the grandparents in 1984 in circumstances not dissimilar to those giving rise
to her more recent apprehension. The girl made allegations of having been
abused sexually by her grandfather and by an uncle, who also resided in the
home of the grandparents. The school psychologist to whom the alleged abuse was
reported advised the appropriate agency, a predecessor to the present
petitioner, which apprehended the child. As required by law the agency applied
to the court for a finding that the child was in need of protection. In
preparation for the court hearing an investigation into the child's allegations
of abuse was conducted and a psychological evaluation of Bridget undertaken.
The investigation uncovered no evidence corroborative of the child's
accusations, but the evaluation did disclose a troubled girl desperately in
need of a proper upbringing. Permanent placement in a home away from the uncle
and grand-parents was recommended.

[
6
]

The mother intervened in the court
proceedings asking that she be permitted to take Bridget to live with her in
Indiana. A study was made of the mother's home and personal situation by
officials of the Department of Public Welfare of De Kalb County, Indiana. It
raised a number of questions and concerns including, in particular, the
mother's ability to assume responsibility for Bridget without undesirable
influence from the grandmother. The mother did not press her intervention, but
participated in a compromise disposition whereby Bridget was returned to the
care of her grandparents subject to supervision by the agency for a six-month
period. This disposition was subject to terms whereby the grand-parents agreed
that they would seek psychological counselling for Bridget and for themselves;
that they would seek a court order appointing them guardians of Bridget; and
that the uncle would move out of and remain away from their home.

[
7
]

The grandparents did obtain some
counselling for Bridget, but there is no evidence from the counsellor presently
before the court. Nor is there any evidence that the grandparents availed
themselves of any counselling service. Certainly the grandparents did not apply
for appointment as Bridget's guardians. After the period of agency supervision
had expired, the uncle moved back into the home of the grandparents.

[
8
]

In May of this year, Bridget made new
allegations of sexual assaults by her uncle following which she was apprehended
again. This time medical examination disclosed physical evidence consistent
with the allegations. The medical officer reported Bridget as being depressed
and angry. Allegedly she attempted to commit suicide. A consultant psychologist
found that the girl's "personality dysfunction implicates primarily
inadequacies in her grandmother's parenting". He recommended lengthy
residential treatment.

[
9
]

The agency's apprehension of Bridget
had been made pursuant to s. 21(1) of the
Child and Family Services Act
,
1985-86 (Man.), c. 8 (
C.C.S.M., c. C80
) ("the Act"), which provides:

21(1) The director, a representative
of an agency or a peace officer who on reasonable and probable grounds believes
that a child is in need of protection, may apprehend the child without a
warrant and take the child to a place of safety where the child may be detained
for examination and temporary care and be dealt with in accordance with the
provisions of this Part.

A "child in need of
protection" is defined in s. 17 of the Act to include a child:

(
b
) in the care of a person

(i) who is unable or unwilling to
provide adequate care, supervision or control of the child, or

(ii) whose conduct endangers or may
endanger the life, health, or emotional well-being of the child

• • • • •

(
c
) who is abused or is in
danger of abuse.

[
10
]

As required by the Act, the agency
applied to the Court of Queen's Bench for a finding that Bridget was in need of
protection and for an order appointing it as the child's guardian. This
application was opposed first by the grandmother and later by a Mrs. Barbara
Pankop, the mother's sister, who lives in Indiana. The grandmother stated in an
affidavit that Bridget was "quite capable of making up a story" and
asserted that, the uncle having moved out of her home again, there was no
reason why the child could not return to her care. The aunt proposed, as an
alternative placement, that Bridget be committed to her care and control. The
agency pressed on with its application and issue was thus joined as to the
child's need of protection and, if protection was found to be needed, the best
arrangements for the child's care. Pending the determination of the issues by
the court, Bridget was placed in a treatment facility approved by the
consultant psychologist.

[
11
]

At a pre-trial conference in June,
1986, the court gave directions that a home study and personal assessment with
respect to Barbara Pankop be obtained; that the child's wishes be ascertained;
and that, pending the trial, the grandmother be afforded access to visit with
Bridget under the supervision of a social worker.

[
12
]

Following the pre-trial conference,
criminal charges were laid against the uncle with respect to the alleged sexual
assaults on Bridget. A preliminary inquiry into those charges was set for
October 23, 1986.

[
13
]

Shortly thereafter, arrangements were
made for Bridget to visit her grandmother. A social worker accompanied her to
the grand-mother's home. Whilst there Bridget asked permission to go to an
adjoining home where a cousin lived. The social worker saw nothing untoward in
this request and permitted her to go. She did not return. About an hour after
Bridget had left, the social worker became anxious. An inquiry of the
grandmother brought the response: "Her mother was here and took her."
Accepting the grandmother's statement, the social worker left the grandmother's
home to report Bridget's disappearance to the police. When he returned to the
grandmother's residence he found no one at home and the car no longer in the
garage.

[
14
]

The agency applied immediately for an
order of temporary guardianship. The only evidence before the court as to the
whereabouts of Bridget was that an agency worker, who telephoned the Barbara
Pankop residence the day after Bridget's disappearance, had been told by the
person answering that Bridget was in Indiana. Where she was and with whom was
not disclosed. The learned judge hearing the application declined to make an
order of temporary guardianship, but did order that the apprehension remain in
place and that, pending receipt of the report requisitioned at the pre-trial
conference as to the suitability of Barbara Pankop's residence as a home for
Bridget, Bridget reside with her aunt.

[
15
]

The first question for the
consideration of this court is whether or not the court has jurisdiction to
make any order with respect to the guardianship or care of Bridget now that she
is, apparently, out of the jurisdiction. The courts of this province have all
of the jurisdiction exercised in 1870 by the English courts of common law and
equity. It is therefore appropriate that reference be made to English as well
as Canadian authorities.

[
16
]

As long ago as 1854 Lord Chancellor
Cranworth considered the jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery over infants who
were not within the jurisdiction of the court. In
Hope v. Hope

(1854),
4
De G.M. & G. 328
at pp. 345-6,
43 E.R. 534
at p. 541,
he said:

... how can the jurisdiction be
exercised in the case of an infant who at the time the jurisdiction is asked is
not within the jurisdiction of the Court? ... It may be that the child is
placed under such circumstances that the jurisdiction of the Court cannot be
exercised over it because no order I might issue could be enforced; but in that
case there is not a want of jurisdiction, but a want of the power of enforcing
it. ... So with an infant abroad; if the parents were also abroad ... I should
never say that I had no jurisdiction over the infant, if it was a British born
subject of Her Majesty, though I might have no means of enforcing the
jurisdiction. Therefore, it is putting the matter on a wrong footing to say,
because the child is out of the jurisdiction, that the Court has no
jurisdiction. In such a case, anybody might, by merely withdrawing himself from
the jurisdiction, escape all liability to it.

[
17
]

Lord Cranworth dealt with jurisdiction
over infants on the basis of citizenship, no doubt because the child in
question was a British subject. Earlier in
Johnstone v. Beattie

(1843),

10 Cl. & Fin. 42
at p. 119,
8 E.R. 657
at p. 687,
Lord Campbell had
expressed the view that residence within the jurisdiction was a sufficient
foundation for the exercise of jurisdiction. He stated:

I do not doubt the jurisdiction of
the Court of Chancery on this subject, whether the infant be domiciled in
England or not. The Lord Chancellor, representing the Sovereign as
parens
patriae
, has a clear right to interpose the authority of the Court for the
protection of the person and property of
all infants resident
in
England.

(Emphasis added.)

[
18
]

The view that ordinary residence within
the jurisdiction is a sufficient basis for the exercise of jurisdiction was
confirmed emphatically by the English Court of Appeal in
Re P. (G. E.) (an
infant)
,
[1965] Ch. 568
. In that case an infant born in Egypt of Jewish
parents was resident in England. The parents had separated. During the week the
child lived with her mother whilst over the week-ends she lived with her
father. One week-end the father flew to Israel with the child and remained
there. The mother applied to the English Court for an order making the child a
ward of the court, but the judge of first instance struck out her application
on the ground that the child was neither a British subject nor physically
present in England. The Court of Appeal restored the application on the basis
that the court had jurisdiction. Lord Denning M.R. stated, at p. 584:

... the Court of Chancery ... takes
under its protection every infant child who is ordinarily resident within the
realm. ...

In support of the test of ordinary
residence, Lord Denning relied, in part, on the decision of the New York
Supreme Court in
People ex. rel. Descollonges v. Descollonges

(1959),

183 N.Y.S. 2d 943
; affirmed
190 N.Y.S. 2d 314 (C.A.)
.

[
19
]

Lord Denning recognized the
difficulties of enforcing any order the court might make in the physical
absence of the child from the jurisdiction, but concluded that for the court to
decline jurisdiction merely because the child had been spirited out of the
jurisdiction would be to sanction the stratagem of the wrongdoer. He expressed
his view in these words at p. 584:

The Crown protects every child who
has his home here and will protect him in respect of his home. It will not
permit anyone to kidnap the child and spirit it out of the realm. Not even its
father or mother can be allowed to do so without the consent of the other. The
kidnapper cannot escape the jurisdiction of the court by such a stratagem. If,
as in this case, it is the father who flies away with the child, the mother is
not bound to follow him to a foreign clime. She can bring her proceedings
against him in England. I know that it will be difficult for her to enforce any
order the court may make. But it is not impossible. The father may have assets
here. Or he may return for a visit. And if she has eventually to apply to the
courts of the foreign country, they will surely respect an order made by the
courts of the ordinary residence — just as we should — for the simple reason that
it is his home and, as such, is entitled to special consideration.

[
20
]

In the same case, Pearson L.J. (as he
then was) justified the jurisdiction based on ordinary residence in the
following language at pp. 588-9:

Suppose, however, that the infant
is, at the time when the relevant proceedings are instituted, ordinarily
resident in this country but temporarily present in some foreign country. He
may be there on holiday, or accompanying his father on a business trip, or he
may have been "kidnapped" from this country and taken to a foreign
country. "Kidnapping" may include any case of a child being taken out
of this country by some person against the wishes of the parents, or by one
parent against the wishes of the other parent, at any rate where some element of
force or deception or secrecy is involved. In my judgment there must be
jurisdiction in such cases for several reasons. First, justice and convenience
require it. It would be absurd and unjust if the wronged parents or parent were
prevented from obtaining relief in the English court by the accident of the
child being abroad on holiday at a particular date, or by the wrongful act of
"kidnapping".

[
21
]

Canadian courts have applied the same
test of ordinary-residence in accepting jurisdiction with respect to the
custody and guardianship of infants who are beyond the territorial jurisdiction
of the court:
see
Elash v. Elash

(1963),
1963 CanLII 406 (SK QB)
,
43 D.L.R. (2d) 599
,
45 W.W.R.
94
;
Re Walker and Walker

(1971),
1970 CanLII 461 (ON HCJ)
,
14 D.L.R. (3d) 155
,
[1970] 3 O.R. 771
,

3 R.F.L. 78
;
Nielsen v. Nielsen

(1970),
1970 CanLII 435 (ON HCJ)
,
16 D.L.R. (3d) 33
,
[1971] 1 O.R.
541
,
5 R.F.L. 313
, and
Harnish v. Harnish

(1978),
1977 CanLII 2604 (SK QB)
,
4 R.F.L. (2d) 105
.

[
22
]

Some earlier Canadian cases, including
the majority
decision of this Court in
Hannon v. Eisler
,
1954 CanLII 243 (MB CA)
,
[1955] 1 D.L.R.
183
,
62 Man. R. 440
,
13 W.W.R. (N.S.) 565
, were cited in support of the
contention that physical presence of a child within the jurisdiction is a
necessary pre-condition to the exercise of jurisdiction with respect to that
child. In none of these cases was ordinary residence considered as a basis for
jurisdiction and only
in
Hannon v. Eisler
was it even arguable that the
children were in fact ordinarily resident within the jurisdiction.
Hannon v.
Eisler
did not involve the wrongful taking of children out of the
jurisdiction and it should not be regarded as authoritative in cases in which a
child continues to be ordinarily resident within the jurisdiction.

[
23
]

It is my view that Bridget is, on the
facts, ordinarily resident in Manitoba. That residence cannot be displaced by a
wrongful removal. That was true in
In Re P. (G. E.), supra
, when the
application to the court was made after the child had been taken from the
jurisdiction. In the case at bar there are even stronger grounds for holding
that the jurisdiction with respect to the child is not lost by reason of her
removal from Manitoba: the issue of her future care was already before the
court when she was removed. Her removal was an affront to the Court of Queen's
Bench, particularly as the grandmother and aunt had already submitted to its jurisdiction.

[
24
]

Counsel for the grandparents argues
that the court in Indiana alone has jurisdiction to decide what arrangements
are best for the future care of Bridget. I have no doubt that so long as
Bridget is within Indiana it is the orders of the courts of that state which
are enforceable. This court, in making any order, must respect the jurisdiction
of the court in Indiana. That is not to say, however, that the court in Indiana
would not show respect for any order this court might make having particular regard
to the greater proximity this court has to recent events in the child's life.
It is upon a reciprocity of respect between the courts in the two jurisdictions
that the child's best interests will be served.

[
25
]

In cases involving custody disputes
between separated parents, Canadian courts have recognized and given effect to
orders of the courts of other jurisdictions from which children had been
wrongfully removed: see
Re Loughran and Loughran

(1972),
1972 CanLII 360 (ON CA)
,
30 D.L.R. (3d)
385
,
[1973] 1 O.R. 109
,
9 R.F.L. 255
, and
Re Firestone and Firestone

(1978),
1978 CanLII 1629 (ON HCJ)
,
90 D.L.R. (3d) 742
,
21 O.R. (2d) 549
,
7 R.F.L. (2d) 93
. This case is
somewhat different in that the dispute is not between competing family members
each capable of providing care for the child, but a dispute between the child's
family and a statutory agency that alleges that the family does not have the
capability of offering the child the care and support she requires. Moreover,
the child's mother and the custodian proposed by the family live in the
jurisdiction to which the child has been taken. In those circumstances it would
be understandable if the court in Indiana were to elect to decide the issue as
to the child's need of protection itself, either treating the petitioner in
these proceedings as a proper party or substituting a local agency with
appropriate authority and powers. If the court in Indiana elects to exercise
jurisdiction the courts in Manitoba must respect the decision it makes.

[
26
]

On the other hand, the court in Indiana
may consider that, because of the circumstances of the child's removal from
Manitoba, the prior invocation of the jurisdiction of the court here and its
proximity to material events in the child's recent history, or the lack of a
suitable substitute for the petitioner (if that be the case), the child should
be returned to this jurisdiction for a determination of the issue as to the
child's need of protection. In that event the court here must not be perceived
as having prejudged the issue as to the needs of the child, an issue which must
be decided on the merits of the case and not by reaction to the wrongful acts
of the family in removing the child.

[
27
]

This court does not know what course
the court in Indiana will consider best in the child's interest. Indeed, unless
the petitioner has status to apply to the court in Indiana for an order of
custody in its favour, there can be no promise that the issue of the child's
need of protection will even be raised there. This court must fashion its order
in such a manner as will ensure that the issue of the child's needs will be
raised and that the court in Indiana has the full range of options open to it.
If the child is returned to this jurisdiction, there should be no outstanding
order which conflicts with the petitioner's entitlement to care for the child
pending a determination of the issue of the child's need of protection.

[
28
]

The status of an agency which has
apprehended a child in this jurisdiction, but not obtained an order of
guardianship, to apply for an order of custody of that child in another jurisdiction
is not certain. To ensure that such status exists the agency should be
appointed guardian of the child. It can be expected that the court in Indiana
will respect such appointment for the limited purpose for which it is made. The
order of guardianship, on a temporary basis, should also be made to protect the
child should she return to Manitoba. The refusal of the learned judge in the
Court of Queen's Bench to make such an appointment was thus, in my respectful
view, an error as was his approval of the aunt's home as even a temporary
residence for the child. The approval was premature and given on insufficient
evidence. It is tantamount to acquiescence in the wrongful taking of the child
from the care of the agency. The order that the child reside with the aunt is
also inconsistent with the order that the apprehension remain in place.

[
29
]

In making an order this court must take
into account the discretion to be exercised by the court in Indiana and the
interim nature of the present proceeding. I would, therefore, propose making a
temporary order of guardianship in favour of the petitioner. The petitioner
should remain the guardian of the child pending the final disposition of the
petition, but subject to displacement by an order of a competent court in Indiana.

[
30
]

I would allow the appeal accordingly,
set aside the order appealed from and substitute an order of temporary
guardianship of Bridget in favour of the petitioner on the terms indicated.

[
31
]

The agency asks for an order that its
costs be paid. The respondents McKee are resident within Manitoba. They opposed
the agency's application for the assistance of the court after the child was
abducted. The McKees have not denied their complicity in the removal of the
child. In my view, they should pay the agency's costs of the application for
temporary guardianship and of the appeal to this court including a factum fee
of $100. To minimize future proceedings, I would fix the total costs payable,
with respect to the proceedings in both courts, at $400 inclusive of the factum
fee and disbursements.

[
32
]

Appeal allowed; order accordingly.
